NCT05918211.what_is_this_study_about: FUEL-2 asks whether a medicine called udenafil can safely help teens with Fontan circulation exercise better. Teens take either the study medicine or a placebo twice a day for 26 weeks (about six months). A placebo looks like the medicine but has no active drug. Each teen has an equal chance of getting either one. Teens, families, and study doctors do not know which one they get. Exercise tests at the start and end measure how much oxygen the body uses.
NCT05918211.who_might_this_be_for: Teens ages 12 through 18 who have had the Fontan procedure may qualify. They must be at least 132 cm tall (about 4 feet 4 inches) and weigh at least 40 kg (about 88 pounds). They must already take medicine to help prevent blood clots. They must also be able to do the exercise tests and meet the study's exercise limits. Some health problems and medicines may rule someone out. These include a recent hospital stay for worsening heart failure or being assessed or listed for a heart transplant. The study team checks the full set of rules to see who can join.
NCT05918211.why_might_this_matter: Some teens with Fontan circulation find exercise hard. This study may help doctors learn whether udenafil can help and what side effects it may cause. The team also checks blood markers linked to liver scarring. Taking part may not help a teen feel better or exercise more easily.
NCT05918211.what_should_families_know: Families should ask about study visits, tests, and possible side effects. Teens and their parent or guardian must agree to take part, as required for the teen's age. The study website says travel costs are covered and families may receive payment for taking part. Ask the team what is covered and how payment works. Families can use the interest form at fuel2study.com to reach the study team. Sources: the provided ClinicalTrials.gov record and fuel2study.com.

NCT06762964.what_is_this_study_about: This study asks whether a medicine called dapagliflozin changes vein pressure in adults whose Fontan circulation is not working well. Adults take either a 10 mg study tablet or a placebo once a day for 12 weeks. A placebo has no active study drug. The group is chosen by chance. Adults in the study and the staff giving treatment do not know which tablet they get. The team checks vein pressure at rest, with feet raised, and during exercise.
NCT06762964.who_might_this_be_for: Adults age 18 or older who have had the Fontan procedure may qualify. They must have shortness of breath due to their heart condition. Vein pressure must reach the study's cutoff at rest or during exercise. The team checks this at the first visit. People below the cutoff cannot join the treatment part of the study. Some health problems and medicines may rule someone out. Examples include type 1 diabetes, a recent hospital stay, serious kidney or liver disease, and pregnancy or breastfeeding. People whose Fontan surgery has been reversed cannot join. The study team checks all the rules.
NCT06762964.why_might_this_matter: The study may help doctors learn how this medicine affects pressure and blood flow in people with Fontan circulation. The team also checks how much people can exercise and how they feel in daily life. Taking part may not improve a person's health or symptoms.
NCT06762964.what_should_families_know: The study is at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. It plans to enroll 27 adults. Tests take place at the start and after about three months. They include heart and exercise tests, a health survey, and scans to measure body fat and other tissue. A blood-volume test uses a radioactive tracer. The first visit includes an invasive vein-pressure test, which involves entering the body. Ask the team how this test is done, what risks the tests and drug have, and what visits and travel may cost. Contact Amanda Wozniak at 507-266-1976 or Wozniak.Amanda@mayo.edu. Source: the provided ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT06762964.

NCT05647213.what_is_this_study_about: This early study tests heart cells grown in a lab from a person's own cells. The main goals are to learn if it is safe to give these cells to people and if the study steps can be carried out. The team compares people who receive the cells with people who do not. This is called a Phase 1 study.
NCT05647213.who_might_this_be_for: This study is for a small group of adults ages 18 through 40 with single ventricle heart disease and very severe heart failure. Their heart must have poor pumping strength despite at least three months of the best available treatment. The rules include a doctor's estimate that the person may have only 1 to 1.5 years to live when the skin sample is taken. They must also face a transplant wait longer than that estimate, have been denied a transplant, or plan to use a heart-support device as long-term care. Other rules apply. Some heart rhythm problems, kidney or liver disease, any past cancer, and a prior heart transplant can rule someone out. The study team reviews each person's case.
NCT05647213.why_might_this_matter: Adults with very severe heart failure may have few treatment options. This study may help doctors learn whether cells made this way are safe enough for more research. It has not shown that the cells help the heart work better or help people live longer. Taking part does not replace the need for other heart care.
NCT05647213.what_should_families_know: The study is at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. It starts with a small skin sample, called a biopsy. It may take about nine months to prepare the heart cells. Getting the cells is not assured: the cells must pass quality checks, and the person must still meet the study rules. People must agree to follow-up for the rest of their lives. Those who receive cells need someone with them day and night for the first three weeks. The rules also require being able to use a heart monitor placed in the body and a wearable device that can treat dangerous heart rhythms. Those who receive cells must be able to take a heart rhythm drug for up to three months. Ask about risks, visits, travel costs, and the help needed at home. Contact HLHS@mayo.edu. Source: the provided ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT05647213.
